planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive soil with access to irrigation; Stevens is the most widely planted commercial cranberry cultivar in North America and is a reliable, high-yielding choice for a home bog bed.

directions: Stevens is a USDA-bred hybrid cranberry cultivar (a cross of Vaccinium macrocarpon selections McFarlin and Potter) that has become the standard commercial variety across North American cranberry-growing regions, prized for large, uniform, deep-red berries, vigorous upright vines, and consistently heavy yields that outperform most older cultivars and many wild bog selections. It requires the same strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), constant moisture, and sandy-peat substrate as other cranberries, mimicking the native bog habitat, and benefits from a 3-4 inch layer of coarse sand mulch to suppress weeds and maintain the ideal rooting surface. Vines take three to four years to establish a meaningful crop but then produce reliably for decades with minimal input beyond consistent moisture and acidic fertility. Harvest in fall once berries turn deep red and bounce when dropped; home growers typically hand-pick rather than using the wet-harvest flooding method of commercial operations.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension — Cranberry Cultivar Guide
Rutgers University Cranberry and Blueberry Research Center

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive soil with access to irrigation; Ben Lear is an early-ripening cultivar, useful for home growers who want to harvest ahead of the main cranberry season.

directions: Ben Lear is an older, widely grown cranberry cultivar selected from a Wisconsin bog in the early 20th century, valued for its early ripening, large dark-red berries, and vigorous, easy-to-establish vines that make it a good choice for home bog beds where an early harvest is wanted. Flavor and color develop earlier in the season than in later-ripening cultivars like Stevens, though total yield per vine tends to run somewhat lower than the most productive modern releases. It requires the same demanding conditions as all cranberries: strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), constant moisture, and a sandy-peat substrate that mimics its native bog habitat, along with a sand mulch layer to suppress weeds and support proper rooting. Vines take several years to establish before cropping heavily, but then perform reliably for decades. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once berries color fully and bounce when dropped, ahead of the main-season harvest of later cultivars.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension — Cranberry Cultivar Guide
Rutgers University Cranberry and Blueberry Research Center
